conventions: ADONAY (Ncmpc + Sp1cs) is split throughout: the noun takes the ASV's supplied 'the' (3.31, 3.36, 3.37) or the vocative 'O' under rule 36 (3.58), and the 1cs suffix is unrepresented in all four places, because the ASV never writes 'my Lord'. The competing reading fuses both morphemes under rule 30 into the single English word 'Lord'; it was not taken, since 'Lord' carries nothing of the suffix and rule 35's test is what the English word carries. BSB reports all four suffixes as represented, which is this convention difference and not an error.

Where the ASV's verb reaches its object through an English preposition and the Hebrew has no object marker and no preposition morpheme to carry that word, the preposition stays inside the verb's unit and the suffix takes only the pronoun: 'call for help' (3.8), 'wait for ... him' (3.25), 'called upon ... thee' (3.55, 3.57), 'rose up against ... me' (3.62). Rule 16 hands such a preposition to H853 only where the marker is present; where it is not, nothing else licenses the word. The competing reading, which gives the preposition to the suffix, is named in the notes at 3.25 and 3.62.

A supplied relative pronoun introducing an asyndetic relative clause joins that clause's finite verb and heads on the lexical verb: 'the man that hath seen' (3.1), 'the soul that seeketh' (3.25), 'the day that I called upon' (3.57). Rules 41 and 46 do not reach these, since no article, participle or asher is present to take the relative. A supplied subordinating conjunction that is not a relative in an argument slot goes the other way and is its own added unit: the 'when' of 3.37 carries a relation no morpheme has. Not promoted to the contract: corpus units in Isaiah put the same supplied relative on a present negative instead (lo as 'that not' ISA.63.8 and ISA.65.1, 'which not' ISA.64.3), so the placement is not settled outside this chapter.

An English 'and' standing between two separately rendered items that no waw joins is added (3.14 between the two predicates, 3.60 and 3.61 between the two objects). An 'and' written inside a single idiomatic English rendering of one morpheme is not: shub rendered 'again and again' (3.3) is one unit, because no part of that phrase belongs to any other morpheme and dropping 'and again' would leave English the ASV wrote unlicensed. Rule 42's surplus-'and' clause is about numerals; this is the same reasoning drawn wider, with rule 30's 'one English rendering, not one English token' marking the boundary.

A determiner the ASV supplies for a noun that has no morpheme to license it joins that noun's unit and is never added, beyond the 'a' rule 15 already covers: a possessive where no suffix morpheme is present ('his cheek' 3.30, 'our hands' 3.41) and a quantifier ('any intermission' 3.49). This does not reach a supplied object pronoun standing inside a verb phrase, which stays added under rule 44 (3.2, 3.5, 3.20, 3.28, 3.37, 3.66); the test is whether the supplied word is the noun's determiner or the verb's argument.
report: Checked all 54 candidate lemma groups. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by what the ASV writes rather than by a difference in analysis: articles split on whether a 'the' is written (aligned at 3.1, 3.3, 3.12b, 3.14, 3.29, 3.41, 3.45, 3.53, 3.62; unrepresented at 3.12a, 3.15, 3.16 twice, 3.23, 3.27, 3.38 twice, 3.44, 3.47 twice, 3.52 - each correct against its own verse); prepositions and conjunctions split on the English word chosen (waw as and/also/that/nor/yet, kiy as For/that/because/when, lamed as to/for/unto/every/at/against/unrepresented); the pronominal suffixes take the pronoun the ASV actually writes. No lemma is analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference.

The candidate table is keyed by source lemma and so is blind to added units, so the dump was read end to end for that family. The chapter's ten added units fall in three groups and each is applied consistently: a supplied object pronoun inside a verb phrase where no object morpheme is present (3.2 t007, 3.5 t008, 3.20 t004, 3.28 t012, 3.37 t015, 3.66 t004); a coordinating 'and' that no waw licenses (3.14, 3.60, 3.61); and the supplied subordinator 'when' (3.37). The counterpart foldings are equally consistent: supplied copulas on the predicate (3.1, 3.10, 3.22, 3.23 twice, 3.24, 3.25, 3.26, 3.27, 3.37, 3.47, 3.52, 3.63), supplied subject pronouns and modals on the verb, supplied relatives on the finite verb (3.1, 3.25, 3.57), supplied determiners on the noun (3.19, 3.25, 3.27, 3.30, 3.41, 3.47, 3.49, 3.55, 3.57).

Two near-misses worth naming because they look like splits and are not. 3.2 and 3.66 each write the object pronoun twice for a single suffix; both give the pronoun to the verb that actually carries the suffix (3.2 the first 'me', 3.66 the second 'them') and mark the other added - one rule producing opposite positions, which is right. And 3.3 folds an 'and' into shub's rendering 'again and again' while 3.14, 3.60 and 3.61 mark a coordinating 'and' added; the difference is that no part of 'again and again' belongs to any other morpheme, so rule 30's fusion (one English rendering, not one English token) covers it, whereas the coordinating 'and' stands beside two separately rendered items. Recorded as a convention rather than patched.

Other families checked and found uniform: light verb plus complement heads on the complement (3.4 'made old', 3.7 'made heavy', 3.9 'made crooked', 3.20 'in remembrance', 3.28 'keep silence', 3.32 'have compassion') while a lexical verb keeps its head (3.8 'call for help', 3.11 'pulled in pieces'); causatives head on the second verb (3.2, 3.6, 3.13); phrasal particles stay with the verb (3.9 'up', 3.11 'aside', 3.17 'far off', 3.30 'full', 3.31 'off', 3.35 'aside', 3.40 'again', 3.48/3.49/3.50/3.63 'down'); rule 31 substantive phrases head on the lexeme (3.6 'dark places', 3.9 'hewn stone', 3.10 'secret places', 3.16 'gravel stones', 3.26 'quietly wait', 3.39 'punishment of sins'); expletive 'there' joins its verb in both places it occurs (3.29, 3.38); construct chains follow rule 29 uniformly, including the two-article case at 3.45.

BSB: none of the twelve disagreements is a genuine error. Four are the ADONAY suffix at 3.31, 3.36, 3.37 and 3.58, where the ASV writes 'the Lord' or 'O Lord' and never 'my Lord'. Two are the paragogic he at 3.59 and 3.63, which rule 32 documents as a standing convention difference. Two are a lamed silenced by ASV recasting under rule 40 (3.44 ethical dative rendered 'thyself', 3.51 object promoted to a bare direct object). Three are articles the ASV writes no 'the' for (3.38 twice, 3.47). One is a suffix the ASV writes no possessive for (3.34 'under foot'). No accepted edge was changed.

No promotion. The one real gap this chapter met is a supplied relative pronoun for an asyndetic relative clause, which rules 41 and 46 do not cover because no article, participle or asher is present; LAM.3 puts it on the finite verb three times (3.1, 3.25, 3.57). The corpus contradicts that placement where a negative is present - lo aligned to 'that not' at ISA.63.8 and ISA.65.1 and to 'which not' at ISA.64.3, all heading on the negative - so a rule saying the finite verb takes it would be contradicted by the corpus it has to live with. Recorded as a chapter convention instead, with the contrary precedent named so a later chapter with wider evidence can settle it.

Rule 53 does not apply: the packet carries no FALLBACK EXCLUDED mark, the three selected textual units (3.20, 3.32, 3.39) are at the base reading, and the single underdetermined unit (3.10 v001, covering ariy) keeps a fallback the English permits. All 66 verses are present in the dump; the ledger totals in the validation report reconcile (598 units, 593 source and 888 target tokens, no missing or duplicated ids).
